supportingExcerpt: Cutting sections moves material from the block onto slides; extraction consumes a portion and loses its original architecture. Stored images and datasets can be copied and reanalysed but cannot refill the archive. A newly collected biopsy is another procedure and time point, and a growing culture is a changed system rather than replenishment of the original specimen.

Specimen allocation starts by identifying the available portions, assessing their suitability, estimating method-specific use and recording consumption. Blocks, slides, frozen pieces and cell aliquots are finite inputs; their counts alone do not establish adequacy. Record remaining portions with section thickness, area or analyte amounts and the relevant context. Receiving-laboratory requirements and diagnostic priorities apply, rather than a universal test budget. Outdated inventories, unrecognised exhaustion, unsuitable regions and duplicated destructive work can waste material. Specimen governance supports reliable testing but is not itself a clinical biomarker and does not establish whether a test changes care or another procedure is appropriate.

Fictional small block: one proposed extraction remains possible after diagnostic needs are protected, while two teams request overlapping RNA tests. Compare questions, validated inputs, existing-data reuse, permissions and expected material use with pathology before allocation. No universal section count, percentage budget or clinical priority follows from this exercise.

NCI biospecimen guidance places pathology oversight of tissue release alongside the need to protect complete medical evaluation. It also treats divided and extracted material as traceable derivative samples. A thoracic small-specimen guideline addresses triage and handling for multiple ancillary studies in its own clinical scope. The general resource issue is finite material, not a universal order of tests: remaining tissue and assay requirements need to be established for the actual specimen.

An aliquot is an allocated portion. Retain site, date, treatment context, preservation, region, quantity, prior uses, remaining material, permissions and custody. A block list or ten remaining slides does not prove that relevant malignant cells remain. Returning a block does not replace extracted tissue.

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded material preserves architecture and supports assays validated for its altered molecules, but cannot restore the original living cells. Snap-freezing preserves material for molecular analysis; the NCI protocol excludes viability, sorting and culture endpoints. A viable-cell vial requires verified recovery, identity and function for its intended assay. No preparation label measures tumour content.

Preparation can irreversibly close options. If fixed molecular assays and living-cell experiments are both contemplated, their inputs and separate aliquots need planning before processing, while protecting diagnostic requirements. There is no universally best preparation; dividing finite tissue also has a cost.

The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Death plus extracellular ATP does not establish a cancer vaccine. Danger signals, cross-priming, functional protection, distant control and patient benefit are separate claims. Even a positive mouse vaccination assay remains model-bound and does not select a clinical treatment.

Class I HLA commonly displays fragments of proteins made within the presenting cell. Cross-presentation means displaying externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Naive CD8 T-cell priming is a further activation step requiring an appropriate presenting cell and supporting signals; tumour-cell display alone does not establish priming. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

Priming is initial activation of a naive T cell. Cross-presentation places externally acquired material on class I HLA in a presenting cell; that event is distinct from a cancer cell naturally displaying a recognised target. Both strategies still need evidence of presentation, suitable priming or expansion, tumour access, useful function, outcomes and harms. Dashed links in a comparison diagram mark questions to investigate, not successful completion of each step.

Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

Division, viable-cell expansion, cytokine production and target-cell death are distinct priming outcomes. In a fictional matched experiment both cultures show three divisions, yet only B kills appropriate targets above target-only background. Measure these outcomes separately with defined starting cells, presenting system, signal perturbation, matched time, peptide loading, HLA, cell ratios and culture conditions. Priming does not establish tumour access, natural display, safe killing or clinical benefit, and stronger stimulation can support unwanted populations.

The strategy uses relevant tumour antigens in place while supporting presenting cells and immune activation. Antigen availability, uptake and processing, cross-presentation, suitable priming, access to another lesion, recognition of naturally displayed targets and useful function are conditional jobs. Local injury can supply material without establishing all these steps, and danger signals alone do not establish immunogenic cell death. An uninjected lesion can still be exposed to systemic drugs.

A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

First define the irradiated field and the actual exposure of each lesion. A local response does not demonstrate a distant response. An uninjected-lesion response in an injection study is a different route-defined observation. During concurrent systemic treatment, distant shrinkage does not by itself isolate radiation’s contribution or demonstrate immune causation; local control, distant response, survival, symptoms and harms require separate assessment.

In a local-treatment study, follow injury and signals through presentation, priming, recognition and measured tumour outcomes. Circulating cytokines or proliferating T cells alone do not establish tumour-specific killing, distant control or an optimal radiation dose.

Serial blood sampling can follow circulating analytes or cell populations over time. Plasma, serum and blood-cell fractions are different inputs. Circulating material does not preserve the local tissue architecture and cell relationships available from a tissue sample.

A second invented comparison starts with ten cells in one square millimetre of viable edge from lesion L. Follow-up A counts ten in the same stated area and region of L, giving ten cells per square millimetre at both times under the supplied assumptions. Follow-up B counts ten in 0.2 square millimetres from an injured centre of lesion M, giving fifty per square millimetre. B does not show a rise within L. Retain the lesion, viable area, centre or edge, collection time, treatment context and counting method. An early sample can capture transient injury signals and a later one a changed surviving-cell mixture. Equal area does not make separate tissue pieces identical, and matched sampling alone still cannot establish recruitment causation.

The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by mononuclear inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and plasma cells, as a percentage of eligible tumour-associated stroma. It is not the percentage of all cells, a CD8-cell count or the fraction of cancer cells being killed.

A fictional sTIL estimate of 30% means that the defined mononuclear infiltrate occupies about 30% of eligible stromal area. It does not mean 30% of all cells are lymphocytes or CD8 cells, or that 30% of cancer cells are being killed. Intratumoral TILs, positive-nucleus fractions, cells per square millimetre and bulk immune RNA measure different things. Additional stains change the measurement rather than silently changing its denominator.

Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Input and tissue cost: a compatible fixed or frozen section; staining uses material and may involve repeated processing, and the section does not preserve viable cells for a killing assay. Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. Failure modes: autofluorescence, overlapping signals, nonspecific antibodies, staining-order effects, tissue loss, alignment errors and incorrect cell boundaries. Cannot establish: all proteins, live-cell behaviour, antigen specificity, actual killing or universal treatment eligibility. Validation: specific to the panel, staining, imaging, analysis and intended use.

Two fictional six-symbol PD-1-positive populations near cancer have different controlled peptide responses: one viral and one tumour-peptide directed. Marker and proximity do not establish specificity; peptide response does not establish natural tumour display, access or killing. Checkpoint blockade does not rewrite receptor specificity. Preserve tissue, sampling time, population definitions and controlled function alongside RNA/protein panels; favourable markers or division alone cannot predict benefit.

Frequency arithmetic, fictional: clonotype A is 10 of 10,000 sampled receptor units at baseline (0.1%) and 20 of 1,000 later (2%). The measured relative frequency rose twentyfold, but these are sampled receptor units and not a census of cells, and other populations contracting, different sampling and method effects can change frequency. Read counts are not always cell counts, because preparation, amplification and transcript abundance can change them, and absolute expansion needs compatible cell-number evidence. A sequence overlap between blood and tumour is detected overlap under a clonotype definition and is not a target, and antigen specificity needs a matching controlled recognition experiment.

A repertoire report can give a clonotype list, relative frequencies, diversity, clonality and overlap, but there is no universal expansion or clonality threshold that proves tumour specificity. A sequence found in dissociated tumour material does not locate its cell inside a cancer-cell nest. Not detected means absent from the assay result under its sampling and calling rules, while an observed overlap or change nominates a receptor for a separate controlled recognition experiment.

RNA is distributed across cellular compartments. Whole-cell and nucleus preparations sample different material and can recover different populations. Barcodes label captured profiles rather than certifying one intact cell; quality, ambient RNA and doublet checks remain necessary. Sparse capture and selective recovery prevent a complete census, and many profiles from one biopsy do not create independent patient replicates.

Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

Assay card for spatial transcriptomics (a reading guide, not a score). Measures and how: RNA with coordinates, by preparing a section, capturing or probing RNA, sequencing or imaging, decoding, registering positions and reporting the assignment rules. Input and tissue cost: protocol-compatible frozen or fixed sections; sectioning and molecular preparation consume allocated material, some workflows alter or destroy the assayed section, and re-scoring existing data consumes no new tissue. Output and units: gene counts per spot, bin or assigned cell, and decoded molecule coordinates, often in micrometres, with physical dimensions, normalisation and observed-versus-imputed labels kept. Thresholds: assay-specific gene or probe coverage, capture and decoding quality, background and segmentation criteria; no universal high-expression or neighbourhood cutoff. Failure modes: poor RNA, incomplete probe coverage, low capture, image-registration errors, inaccurate segmentation, spillover and unsuitable reference models. Limits: no automatic single-cell identity, complete transcriptome, whole-tumour representation, proven interaction or clinical selection rule. Validation tier: many workflows are research methods, so check analytical and intended-use validation for the exact assay and model; resolution claims and regulatory status are separate questions.

Method limit, finite input: the plasma volume drawn is not the volume or the number of molecules recovered and evaluated. Low molecular counts, changes in background DNA, poor recovery or incompatible calibration all limit comparison across assays, and a printed zero is not a count of zero cancer cells anywhere in the body.

Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. Both samples are called detected, but the second is below the assay's reliable quantitation range. The printed estimates fall by two-thirds; they do not establish that the cancer volume fell by two-thirds. Retain the qualifying calls and uncertainty, because shedding and background DNA can change the signal. A second method reporting molecules per millilitre cannot simply be placed on this fraction scale. Even a matching unit label does not establish matching calibration. Keeping serial methods and input comparable helps interpretation without removing biological variation.

Source attribution comes first: a positive plasma variant may come from a blood-cell clone rather than a tumour. In Razavi's paired sequencing, 53.2% of cell-free DNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, so a discordant positive needs origin checks before it is read as occult disease.

Fictional matched receptor samples contain 10 clonotype A cells among 1,000 T cells (1%) and 10 among 100 (10%). The sampled count remains 10; the changed denominator drives the larger fraction. Absolute expansion requires comparable sampling and calibrated counts, and neither frequency identifies antigen. State sampling depth, chain definition, compartment, method and timing.

Method card, what it measures: light scatter and fluorescence from individual events in a prepared cell suspension, grouped by a chosen panel of stains. Input: whole blood, isolated cells or dissociated tissue, where preparation and staining use a defined aliquot and compatibility with later assays depends on fixation and other processing and tissue dissociation removes geography and can recover cell types unevenly. Output: event counts, percent of a named parent population, fluorescence in instrument-dependent units, and cells per volume only with a validated counting method. Controls: instrument checks, unstained and single-stain controls, viability, biological controls and fluorescence-minus-one controls for hard boundaries. Failure modes: dead cells, aggregates, weak markers, nonspecific staining, signal overlap, cell loss and inconsistent gates. It cannot tell unmeasured proteins, original tissue position, antigen specificity from general markers or benefit.

A cytokine name does not specify one outcome: one cytokine can act differently on different receiving cells (pleiotropy), different signals can give overlapping outputs (redundancy), and receptor availability, concentration, exposure time and cell state all shape the response.

Retain collection time, treatment context, tube, processing delay, fraction, storage, input quantity, assay and detection limit. Repeat collections have practical burdens and provide later biological time points. Comparisons require compatible methods and the same named question.

Use the blood collection date and imaging acquisition date to compare biology, then keep the reporting dates as a separate measure of when the information became available. Imaging does not remove a tissue aliquot for molecular analysis; contrast or tracer use belongs to the specific protocol. Agreement can reflect shared dependence on disease burden and is not two independent proofs of the same mechanism. Combining measurements into a decision rule needs validation of the combination and its intended outcome.

Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.

Adding receptor measurements introduces another question to a blood and imaging comparison. A sequenced clonotype's sampled abundance does not directly measure its antigen, effector activity or total cell count. Even a controlled secretion or killing result belongs to its tested stimulus and targets. Collecting the measurements together does not link a particular receptor to the tumour DNA signal. Retain time, compartment, chain definition, abundance unit, controls and independent target-recognition evidence; combining the results does not make a validated treatment rule.

In a fictional comparison using compatible measurements, tumour DNA is stable or rising in two patterns and falls in two others, while a receptor measure changes little or increases. Stable or rising DNA with little repertoire change raises questions about the tumour, immunity and assay adequacy without diagnosing resistance or mandating a tissue or spatial test. With greater repertoire change it still does not prove a physical barrier or an antigen-specific response that failed. Falling DNA with little repertoire change does not assign the effect to chemotherapy or show that useful immunity is absent. Falling DNA with greater repertoire change does not prove that immune learning caused control. These are sampled observations, not validated best-response categories, proof of clinical benefit or instructions to change treatment.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

Scatter and marker panels help define populations under the stated assay, but scatter alone does not uniquely identify a cell type. Low event numbers and rare populations need uncertainty and acceptance rules appropriate to the panel and purpose. A gate boundary, minimum event count or research cluster is not a universal clinical-response threshold, and analytical reproducibility of the panel does not establish treatment benefit.
